speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Chairman, let me thank Members for their continued commitment to a strong defence for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I note the speeches that many Members in this House have given during the Budget Debate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is particularly gratifying and reassuring for our future, for Singapore's future, that despite Defence, Security, Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs accounting for one-third of our expenditure, that we have got support across the aisle, across parties.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I think that is a strong signal that the future for Singapore bodes well.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Last year was a busy year for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We staged a number of key events on international efforts on the world stage, and in response to Mr Vikram Nair and Ms Sylvia Lim, Singapore's image and standing, because we played host, were enhanced, but it also called for extra and stringent security measures here.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In June, Members would remember that the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) deployed at short notice – it was yes, on-off, on-off – and in two weeks, we were asked to host the United States (US)-Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) Summit.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our efforts, together with those of the Home Team, proved a deterrent to would-be provocateurs.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The SAF mounted a similar operation when Singapore hosted the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in November where all the ASEAN Heads of Government and many other foreign dignitaries gathered.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That meeting, we galvanised the ADMM and ADMM-Plus countries to address common security concerns, including counterterrorism and Chemical, Biological and Radiological Defence threats, and we facilitated ASEAN’s adoption of Indonesia’s “Our Eyes” Initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is an initiative which can enhance regional counterterrorism information-sharing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And Singapore will assist Indonesia to set up and operate this facility.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: GAME can prevent disastrous consequences that can result from unplanned encounters between military aircraft in the air.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have also worked on putting the Code for Unplanned Encounters at Sea (CUES) – some Members asked about this – it has been put into practice across all ADMM-Plus navies, including during the inaugural ASEAN-China Maritime Exercise in October last year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Later this year, we will use CUES for the ADMM-Plus Maritime Security Exercise, which will include both the US and China.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: All in all, Singapore did its fair share to enhance regional security and stability.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: On that score, it was a productive and fruitful year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In the last few months though, we have had our challenges with Malaysia.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng had asked about this.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Even now, two Malaysian government vessels continue to be anchored in our territorial waters off Tuas.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Singaporeans and Members are familiar with these developments and I need not elaborate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Suffice to say, we have strongly cautioned Malaysia to withdraw their vessels.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In fact, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' (MFA’s) press statement in December last year pointed out that, I quote, “Malaysia’s deployments in this area will not strengthen its legal claim and can only heighten tensions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Malaysia will be responsible for any untoward situations on the ground that arise from continued deployment of its vessels into this area.” And indeed, just as we warned could happen, last month, the Greek bulk carrier Pireas collided with the Malaysian government vessel Polaris.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mercifully, no bodily harm ensued, but it could have been much worse.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Singaporeans will remember the collision between the USS McCain and the oil tanker Alnic off Pedra Branca in August 2017, where 10 crewmen perished.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Even so, some in Malaysia have accused Singapore of orchestrating the collision with the Polaris.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These false accusations would have been much louder and strident to push for retaliation against Singapore and Singaporeans, if lives had been lost in the recent collision.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our MFA and the Ministry of Transport (MOT) officials are meeting for discussions and negotiations and the presence of these Malaysian government vessels does not help in any way and, in fact, exposes them to danger and obstructs productive talks.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: MPA, PCG and RSN are closely monitoring activities in Singapore’s territorial waters off Tuas 24/7 and will remain ever vigilant to guard our sovereignty and rights under international law.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: MINDEF will continue its efforts in defence diplomacy.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members have asked that, including Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Vikram Nair.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We want to promote regional peace and stability.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We make friends with those who are willing, and partner those countries whose interests are aligned with ours and who share our desire for inclusiveness, peaceful resolution of disputes and respect for the law.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But at the same time, we must ensure that the SAF is strong and adequate to defend our rights when diplomacy fails and when others choose to do us harm or ignore our rights.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As Prof Fatimah Lateef said, "A strong SAF protects Singapore and Singaporeans." And it has been our persistent investments and efforts to build the Next-Generation SAF that can better respond to the security threats for another generation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These developments are progressing well and I would like to elaborate on that because many Members of Parliament have asked how do we respond to different scenarios of threats that will come upon us in this generation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And we have to prepare for the future because it takes that period of time to build up that kind of SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members have asked for more details on our modernisation of the Next-Generation SAF – Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Pritam Singh, Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Chong Kee Hiong and Mr Charles Chong – so, let me elaborate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our plans to build the Next-Generation SAF to better respond to security threats are progressing well for all three services.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Henry Kwek has asked about the F-35s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have announced our plans to replace the F-16s, which will face obsolescence post-2030, with the F-35s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This will mean that the Republic of Singapore Air Force (RSAF) fighter fleet will consist of F-35s and F-15SGs, if plans come to fruition a decade or so from now.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As stated previously, MINDEF will issue a Letter of Request (LOR) to the US to acquire F-35s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As required by US law for foreign military sales, the US Congress must approve the sale of F-35s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Singapore has the endorsement of both the US Administration and the Department of Defense for our proposed purchase of F-35s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, President Trump wrote to Prime Minister Lee last month welcoming Singapore's plans to acquire the F-35s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: During my meeting with Acting Secretary of Defense, Patrick Shanahan at the Munich Security Conference two weeks ago, he also said that the US was greatly appreciative of Singapore's decision and his department supported it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The price of F-35s has been steadily falling due to healthy orders from the US and 10 other countries, including the United Kingdom (UK), Italy, Australia, Japan and South Korea.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Defence Science and Technology Agency's (DSTA's) assessment is that now is an opportune time to put in Singapore's request.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Total Cost of Ownership of a fleet of F-35s, including maintenance across its lifespan, will also be similar to our F-15SGs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Nonetheless, MINDEF will continue to work with the US Department of Defense to optimise operating and maintenance costs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: RSAF will also take delivery of new helicopters from 2020 onwards.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The H225M medium-lift and our Chinook heavy-lift helicopters will replace our existing Super Puma and CH-47D fleets.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These new helicopters will add capacity and be more effective in Search and Rescue or Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For RSN, our submarines in operation are over two decades old.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will replace them with four new Invincible-class submarines.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The first was launched recently in Germany, with the other three being built.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Invincible-class submarines will have longer endurance, and also the latest locally-developed sensors and automated systems designed for optimal use in our surrounding waters.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have launched our submarines lately in Kiel, facing the North Sea.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We launched our previous class of submarines in the Baltic Sea.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For surface ships, our ageing missile corvettes have served with distinction since 1989.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They are also "Pioneer Generation" that will have to be retired soon, and they will be replaced by the new Multi-Role Combat Vessels (MRCVs).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: More than just improving capabilities, the new MRCVs will incorporate many new ideas.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First of all, they will use less manpower.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Many Members of Parliament have pointed out how we will deal with the one-third reduction in manpower.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The MRCVs will use less manpower, about half the size of that found in modern frigates.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is possible because we designed it from the onset, custom-built for lean manning, using technologies which automate many functions, including maintenance.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As a result, there is also a cost saving of up to 10% in operating them, compared to other similar-sized frigates.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The MRCVs will also have more unmanned air and sea drones.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, it would not be just a manned ship, it will have air and sea drones and modular packages to extend their reach and flexibility against threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Many Members are familiar with our Landing Ship Tanks (LSTs).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think many Members have sailed on them and they proved their worth time and again.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Each time we deploy them in exercises, we say we are so grateful that we have this platform.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So versatile and able to meet mission objectives.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It has been the workhorse in our humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR) efforts and other missions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The LSTs are ageing, too, and will need to be replaced in the next decade by larger and more flexible Joint Multi-Mission Ships.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the Army, the Next-Generation Armoured Fighting Vehicle will replace our M113 Ultras as the mainstay of the SAF's mechanised forces from this year onwards.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Singaporeans will see them soon on our roads at this year's National Day Parade.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These Armoured Fighting Vehicles have better armour protection and mobility through urban environments.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Another addition to the Army will be the Next-Generation Howitzers with extended range and greater precision strikes compared to our current platforms.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have talked about air, land and sea manned platforms, but the signature change for the SAF 2030 and beyond is that the SAF will become more of a hybrid force.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some of the RSAF's unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have been operating for more than a decade.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They will be replaced by newer UAVs with better capabilities over the next few years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I mentioned the MRCVs and unmanned surface vessels, too.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But in the Army, soldiers within the Army will soon use micro-UAVs, your own UAV or the UAV for your unit, for the first time, which will be particularly useful in built-up and urban environments.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These unmanned platforms will complement traditional manned equipment, to enhance responses across a full range of operational scenarios.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In all, the Next-Generation SAF of 2030 and beyond, with this full complement of assets in air, land and sea, will be able to defend Singapore for another generation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is the SAF that will take us into and guard our future.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is the SAF that our investments have bought or will buy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is the SAF on air, land and sea with which the next generation of Singaporeans will celebrate for SG75.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: By then, we will have a state-of-the-art coastal surveillance network and air defence systems to form a shield around Singapore against incoming threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: RSAF will fly F-35s and F-15SGs over our skies, supported by A330 Multi-Role Tanker Transport aircraft, G550 Airborne Early Warning Aircraft, new helicopters and a host of new UAVs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: RSN will have MRCVs, Invincible-class submarines, new unmanned surface vessels and larger Joint Multi-Mission Ships, in addition to existing frigates and Littoral Mission Vessels.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Army will be more protected and mobile, with soldiers mounted in Next-Generation Armoured Fighting Vehicles and Terrex Motorised Vehicles.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Leopard tanks, HIMARS and Next-Generation Howitzers will support them, complemented by a full suite of combat engineers, signals, logistics and maintenance platforms.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But hardware alone would not build you a strong army and a strong military.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will have to have new training facilities both here and overseas which will ensure that our National Servicemen (NSmen) and Regulars can build a modern and capable SAF that can defend Singapore and our interests.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I know Members here have asked that, Mr Zainal Sapari, amongst others.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF of 2030 and beyond has been designed to be operated with a leaner manpower pool.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng, Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Mr Zainal Sapari and Mr Pritam Singh asked about this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have already mentioned the MRCVs for the Navy which need a smaller crew.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, it is a significant reduction, and yet the Next-Generation Howitzer will fire more rounds accurately per minute.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Autonomous and automated systems will reduce labour-intensive tasks, for example, runway damage assessment of our air bases and air strips.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The modern systems and platforms of the SAF can also be operated by NSmen who are not Physical Employment Standard (PES) A or B and, therefore, effectively increase our utilisation of manpower pool.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Pari passu with the acquisition of hardware, we will also invest more into training facilities for SAF soldiers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I last spoke to this House about the SAF Training Institute (SAFTI) City in 2017.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Pioneer and Merdeka Generations are all too familiar with the old SAFTI – you would remember FOFO Hill, Peng Kang Hill, the Pasir Laba Boat Shed and Elephant Hill.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We charged up them and sometimes charged down them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SAFTI City will complement these traditional terrains with urban settings to better prepare our soldiers for a wide variety of operations in the 21st century.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We talked about our SMART City; we are hoping that SAFTI City will be a smart training ground.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will use more simulation and detailed monitoring to help our soldiers to learn better.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will be a far cry from the days that we did our NS and charged up hills or against enemy battalions shouting, "Bang, bang, bang, bang!", and they shouted, "Bang, bang, bang, bang!" back.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For instance, our fighter pilots have been using this for decades to train for high-speed manoeuvres.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: After every manoeuvre, they sit down and say, "All right, you say what you did, he says what he did." This is the objective.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They showed the tracks, they showed where your weaknesses are.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And they have been able to do that because planes are expensive and pilots even more so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But it is only now that modern technology allows us to scale this up for the same processes for individual soldiers within the Army.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, we have been doing this over the years where you can no longer assume that you have hit the target, and you actually have electric sensors on soldiers, on platforms, and the attrition rate is real.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I am glad to report that SAFTI City is taking shape and is on schedule.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will build more roads and bridges so that motorised and mechanised troops in the Army vehicles can start training this year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But with this kind of SAF for 2030 and beyond we can move great distances.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our Terrexes can move 70 kilometres per hour (km/h), and our Leopards close to that, slower perhaps across more difficult terrain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But if we only had space to train in Singapore, you could reach one end to the other within less than an hour.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In particular, the training areas at Shoalwater Bay will be expanded.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There will be new developments in the Townsville Region in Northeast Australia.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I said that very quickly, but an air-land range is priceless.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We can only do this in very few places now – some in the US because they have the land.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is a battlefront that we cannot choose to ignore or we ignore it at our peril.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Charles Chong, Mr Desmond Choo, Prof Fatimah Lateef and Dr Tan Wu Meng have spoken about this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I spoke to this House about the threat of hybrid warfare and its effect on the real world previously.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have seen this played out against the Baltic States and Ukraine, to name some.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And as a culturally and ethnically diverse nation, we, too, are vulnerable to such hybrid attacks, including targeting of our information technology (IT) networks to disrupt services and capabilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members have asked what is our progress of protecting this front and building up a force to protect this front.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Two years ago, I announced the set-up of the Defence Cyber Organisation (DCO).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: DCO has stood up the Defence Cyber Security Centre.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In other words, we have this Defence Cybersecurity Centre within MINDEF and SAF for daily operations against cyber threats against MINDEF and SAF IT systems, especially our command-and-control computer networks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In place are incident response teams which can also be deployed to support other national agencies during cyberattacks on critical systems.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But full-time NSmen (NSFs), too, can play an important part in digital defence, just as they do for kinetic operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think that was the point by Mr Zainal Sapari and Mr Vikram Nair.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Just as we have done for kinetic operations – many of you are familiar with our SAF firing ranges, many of you have fired there – well, we have a cyber range as well – the Cyber Defence Test and Evaluation Centre.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In this cyber range, our cyber soldiers are exposed to realistic training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have created a mock-up, a simulation of the SAF’s networks and online traffic, and we use actual malware and attacks against these nodes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Like in live firing ranges, you are supposed to shoot straight, the SAF aims to train soldiers that can respond to these attacks in a realistic and challenging environment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SAF will also tap on NSmen with IT expertise as a result of their civilian jobs or training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: One example is the existing NS Expertise Conversion Scheme.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It allows non-officer NSmen with industry expertise to become MDES officers for cyber vocations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF and SAF are exploring better matching of NSmen with their civilian IT vocations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All of us have a part to play in Digital Defence for Total Defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In Singapore’s digital fortress, we are only as strong as the weakest link, and Senior Minister of State Mohamed Maliki will share more.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These acquisitions in hardware and facilities, together with the will and skills of our NSmen and NSFs that make up the bulk of the SAF, will put us in a good position to deal with security challenges for another generation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If all these plans come to pass – and I will add that it will take us 10 to 15 years – SAF will be one of the more capable militaries in the region.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our NSFs and NSmen will be able to train well and, most importantly, must train safely.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Inspector-General for Safety has been recently appointed and the office expanded with more safety officers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A number of Members talked about safety – Mr Charles Chong, Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Mr Zainal Sapari.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Commanding Officers of individual units have also been charged with the responsibility and accountability of safety standards and outcomes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As a routine, the Commanding Officer will identify activities each day that pose higher safety risks to his servicemen and women, and satisfy himself that the safety response plan and mitigating measures for such activities are adequate.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Safety is, more than ever, a command responsibility, but each soldier must play his role, too.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we are doing this so that we can have realistic training because, if you cannot train safely, you will be set back.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How will address in greater detail the measures the SAF will take to achieve zero training fatalities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF has also decided to build a central facility to better respond to the needs of the NS community.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will bring together different services which are now scattered across Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For example, today, pre-enlistees take their Individual Physical Proficiency Test (IPPT) at, say, Toa Payoh Stadium, then go to Depot Road Central Manpower Base, and then attend medical reviews at the Military Medicine Institute (MMI) in Kent Ridge.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The new NS Hub will take all these services scattered across the island and put them into a central location.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will be opposite Cashew Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) station, with easy access.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The NS Hub will be built as a smart complex using modern technology for a seamless, user-friendly experience.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Do not worry, we will not take it from anybody.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How will elaborate on the other measures to enhance the NS experience.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To develop such a capable SAF that I have just described, which can protect Singapore’s interests and keep Singaporeans safe for another generation, will require significant and steady investments.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I am grateful to Members of this House and Singaporeans for their steadfast and unwavering support towards a strong SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The commitment that I have put over the next decade of 3% to 4% holds despite this year's increase.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There were just certain projects or acquisitions that have matured and, therefore, we have to spend more.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, the overall defence expenditure will even out in subsequent years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Defence, especially for a small island like Singapore, is crucial if we are to safeguard our interests and deter aggression.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If we continue our steady investments into defence and our NSmen maintain their commitment and resolve to defend Singapore, then our future will be secure for another generation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We can look forward to celebrate SG75 with the assurance that we have strong defences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mr Chairman, Minister for Defence Dr Ng Eng Hen has just spoken about the need for NSmen to train well and to train safely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Indeed, the strength of NS is contingent upon the fighting spirit of our NSmen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our servicemen must undergo tough and realistic military training for the SAF to be an effective fighting force capable of safeguarding Singapore’s sovereignty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, a strong SAF that can defend Singapore must be built without compromising the safety of those serving.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mr Charles Chong asked about balancing operational readiness and safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We understand the anxiety of our soldiers and their families arising from the recent training-related incidents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: MINDEF and SAF take the trust, confidence and expectations that Singaporeans have in our NS system seriously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The External Review Panel on SAF Safety is a standing panel commissioned to assess the SAF’s safety management systems and help ensure that the SAF’s standards and processes are sound and aligned with industry best practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: More recently, the External Review Panels for Heat Injury Management and the External Review Panel for Combat Vehicle Safety were convened in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They assessed the safety procedures to prevent heat injuries and to ensure the operational safety of vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Where shortcomings are discovered, SAF has and will sharpen safety measures to further reduce the risks and to prevent recurrences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Just as a further point, the Army will strengthen training supervision and enhance safety equipment to improve combat vehicle safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These and other specific measures that we shared in this House, we will implement them as soon as possible, and some have already been implemented.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We will not only address individual incidents but will seek to enhance training safety at every level of responsibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim asked about how the SAF is strengthening safety culture at all levels of the SAF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This Office, led by the Chief of Staff – Joint Staff, reports to the Chief of Defence Force and the Permanent Secretary of Defence to enforce safety procedures and to reinforce safety consciousness and culture from the highest level so as to ensure that command emphasis on safety is consistently applied.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On the ground, SAF has renewed the focus of commanders on safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Commanders have comprehensively reviewed safety management plans and the overall training tempo.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They know that they must lead by example in driving safety as a topmost priority.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We want, through concrete action, to reassure Singaporeans that training safety is a top priority for MINDEF and SAF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Ultimately, safety involves everything that I have mentioned, but it also involves more than sound systems and top-down measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Safety must be part of our organisational culture, one that every soldier at every level has a role to own, to build and to foster.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Open reporting means that any servicemen can, at any time, report risky behaviour or near-misses and safety breaches.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And the servicemen know that they can do so without any fear of penalty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They can call the 24-hour safety hotlines for the Army, Navy and the Air Force, and caller identities are kept anonymous.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There are other measures by which they can also surface the feedback.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, the open reporting is about wanting to engender and to ensure openness in the culture, that you are encouraged, indeed, to bring this up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On enlistment day, recruits are briefed by commanders on how they can report safety breaches.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Prior to training, soldiers can identify safety risks using risk assessment checklists and raise concerns to their superiors in a small group setting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This encourages them to look out for their own and their buddies’ safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Since last year, SAF has been developing an application called "SafeGuardian", which will allow SAF servicemen to use their mobile phones to report workplace hazards and instantly share them with other servicemen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, when servicemen are in camp, if they notice, for example, some sharp wire fittings that could potentially cause injury, then that serviceman can take a photo of that using the "SafeGuardian" app and inform the relevant SAF safety officers, so that immediate action can be taken to remove that hazard and to remove that risk.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It will be implemented in phases to the rest of the SAF as soon as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This effort will help enhance safety consciousness and reinforce the point that safety is "By All, For All".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked if we could recognise fallen servicemen, including erecting a memorial.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: SAF honours our servicemen and women who die in service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Every year, SAF observes a minute of silence at the SAF Day Parade to remember our fallen soldiers in the presence of our President or the Prime Minister as the Reviewing Officer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Individual units or formations also hold remembrance events to honour those among their ranks who perish during operations or training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We will never forget their sacrifice to keep Singapore free from those who want to do us harm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On this note, we also want to thank all our NSmen for their commitment and dedication.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Allow me now to speak on how we will enhance the experience for our NSmen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari asked about the importance of NS to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Securing Singapore’s freedom is a sacred duty shouldered by our NSmen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is only right that we continually think of ways to support them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our NSmen have to balance personal and NS commitments, and we must strive to increase convenience for them by reducing administrative burdens wherever possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This will help them focus on the training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We will also maximise the potential and tap into the abilities of our increasingly better-educated pool of servicemen, so that they can contribute even more meaningfully.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng had asked for updates on our efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our operationally-ready NSmen (ORNS) are required to notify the MINDEF Notification Centre and Home Team Overseas Notification Centre of their overseas travel of less than six months' duration, which can currently be done via the NS Portal or by text.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Servicemen just have to keep their contact details, including temporary contact information, updated on the NS Portal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Removing this requirement will not compromise operational readiness, because other exit control measures, such as the requirement to apply for an Exit Permit before traveling overseas for periods of six months or longer, will continue to apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Control measures could be tightened if the need arises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked how we intend to maximise our manpower resource with falling cohort sizes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Besides better technology, equipment, process and job redesign and training of the NSmen, many NSmen also have very relevant and important niche civilian expertise in fields that are relevant both to the civilian side as well as to the military, for example, in nursing or infocommunications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NSmen with such expertise can now contribute to defence with their civilian expertise earlier in their ORNS training cycle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Another example: pre-enlistees are screened at the SAF Medical Classification Centre prior to enlistment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They will then be assigned an appropriate PES grade, so that each person can serve the nation based on his capacity and capabilities, and this would include NSFs with disabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For instance, soldiers with hearing impairment or musculoskeletal disabilities, where found suitable, are assigned to support or administrative vocations, where they are deployed safely and are able to also contribute very meaningfully during their NS stints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We certainly also value the contributions from women to national defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Since 2014, women have served in the SAF Volunteer Corps in areas that support the SAF’s operational and training requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our pool of SAF volunteers comprises a good mix of males and females, with about half being women.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mr Arasu Duraisamy asked about our partnerships to support skills upgrading.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NSFs from SAF and the Home Team dedicate two years to focus on full-time training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Today, certain soldiering, firefighting and rescue competencies are accredited under the Workforce Skills Qualification standard.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To keep pace with the national focus on skills mastery, we seek to support the NSFs’ transition to higher education or into the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: What can our NSFs, therefore, look forward to under these partnerships?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, more resources for skills upgrading after full-time NS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Today, NSFs are granted $350 worth of e-credits for them to subscribe to about 200 online courses, that is, the course list, and these courses are offered by our local universities and polytechnics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We are also working with Institutes of Higher Learning to offer customised courses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NSFs may take these courses to obtain credit exemptions from relevant diploma or degree programmes after they complete their full-time NS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: E-credits can also be used for these courses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For example, NSFs can use their e-credits to take a course on "Introduction to Cloud Architecture" that is offered by the Temasek Polytechnic (TP).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Upon admission to TP’s part-time Specialist Diploma in Cloud Data Centre Technology and Management, participants who complete these online courses will be granted partial exemption from one module.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This will go some way towards supporting our NSFs’ learning journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This month, MINDEF/SAF will co-deliver a career orientation experience with SkillsFuture Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This initiative is supported by our five Community Development Councils and the National Trades Union Congress Employment and Employability Institute (e2i).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We conducted a pilot of this career orientation workshop at Jurong Camp.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: One of our combat engineers, 21-year-old Corporal Ritesh Kumar, said the workshop helped him understand the various pathways available after he completes his full-time NS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: He felt that this gave him and his buddies more useful guidance about their next stage in life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We will take in our servicemen’s feedback and suggestions to refine and improve the SkillsFuture@NS effort in the years ahead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked about our plans to engage the community on NS issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, I want to express our thanks to the Advisory Council on Community Relations in Defence (ACCORD) members for their valuable contributions towards the mission of working with educational institutions, businesses and community groups to strengthen community and total support for our defence and NS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: One of the highlights through the good work of ACCORD in 2018 was the inaugural Women’s Boot Camp.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, in the end, 103 were accommodated for this two-day one-night camp.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That camp gave the women participants, whom I understand have ages that range from 13 to 64.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, in there, there are daughters, mothers, sisters, wives, girlfriends, friends of servicemen, and what they got was a glimpse of military life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They came out seeing NS as tough, but necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: One of them is 50-year-old Ms Koh Wee Min.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: She is a mother of one of our NSFs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: When asked about her experience, Ms Koh said that it gave her a taste of some aspects of military life through participation in iconic NS activities, such as clearing the Standard Obstacle Course.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: She said, "I can now support my son emotionally and psychologically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It will also allay some concerns I have about training safety as I could see that safety is paramount to their training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is reassuring to know that servicemen will get progressive training before they tackle more challenging tasks." This year, we will run another camp so as to continue to engage our community and also this very important constituency, namely, the other half of our population, the women, so that, together, we can strengthen this support for NS and for the defence of our country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our servicemen have told us that sharing photographs of their NS experiences in camp would also help them build a stronger sense of community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Over time, the repository will catalogue the experiences throughout the NS journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If proven successful, we will expand the initiative.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Mr Chairman, the success of NS is measured by the peace safeguarded and maintained, day in, day out, year after year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Every day of peace that Singapore enjoys is testament to the effectiveness of our deterrence, diplomacy and defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: With a strong and resilient NS system that enjoys wide and deep public support, we can continue to be confident about Singapore’s future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Mr Chairman, Minister for Defence Dr Ng Eng Hen has spoken about the uncertain and volatile geopolitical environment that confronts us, and how a strong SAF is vital to help us navigate this landscape for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: History has shown us that having a strong defence makes all the difference.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This is why our long-term and sustained investment in the SAF and Total Defence is vital for Singapore’s continued security and prosperity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: When Total Defence was first introduced in 1984, it was in response to a threat landscape where warfare was very much conventional.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: However, even then, there was a recognition that potential aggressors would target not just the military, but the entire population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As threats evolve, Total Defence becomes even more critical.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They even fund and instruct their members and sympathisers to launch terror attacks like suicide bombings in their own countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: ISIS may have lost ground in the Middle East, but links to our region remain alive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The return of foreign fighters exacerbates this threat.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In this age of the Internet and social media, the resilience of Singaporeans will be tested through attacks from the digital front.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This will be the new battlefront because of how connected we are, and how reliant we are on digital technology to communicate and to consume information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Many examples in Singapore and overseas illustrate the devastating impact that these threats can wreak.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The Digital Dangers and the Need for Strong Digital Defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Citizens could not access cash machines and online banking services; news could not be printed nor broadcasted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: More than 10 years on, cyberattacks in various forms remain a tool for those who would do harm to us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Another example, in July 2018, more recently, the Alaskan borough of Matanuska-Susitna or Mat-su, was, as a British Broadcasting Corporation article describes, sent “back in time” by a malware attack which forced them offline, resulting in some borough staff having to bring out old typewriters just to keep services going.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Another challenge is how quickly information – and disinformation – can spread over the digital domain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The recent riots that broke out at a Hindu temple in Subang Jaya, Malaysia, showed how the spread of rumours and fake news via social media just overnight could fan the flames of racial tensions, and incite social unrest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As Ms Joan Pereira noted, it is important for us to keep our Social Defence strong, so that we stay united against any attempts to divide us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: All communities and faiths have worked hard to build our multicultural and multi-religious society today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We must not let falsehoods pit different social groups against one another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Many of these digital dangers show that complacency, ignorance or negligence on the part of individuals could pave the way for an attack with disastrous consequences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: A January 2019 report by the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's (NATO’s) Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence outlined how their researchers managed to track and trick NATO troops using open-source data primarily from social media.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It was concerning how it was so easy for the researchers to identify troops, locate their battalions, persuade them to abandon their posts and reveal sensitive details about military manoeuvres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Dr Teo Ho Pin asked about our Digital Defence efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We want to bring across the message that every individual is at the forefront of Digital Defence, and this is not a cliché.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is of great significance and, as articulated in an editorial in The Straits Times, and I quote, “every citizen is a soldier in the digital war”, unquote.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Only if everyone plays a part – the Government, businesses, communities and individuals – can we make Digital Defence a part of Singapore’s DNA and keep our defence total.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As a whole-of-nation effort, MINDEF has been working with various Government agencies to fortify Singapore and Singaporeans against digital threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The Ministry of Communications and Information and its agencies, the Cyber Security Agency, the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the National Library Board (NLB) have in place various programmes to empower individuals, businesses and the wider community, so that they can play a part by being secure, alert and responsible online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), the Singapore Police Force has developed further its capabilities to deal with cybercrime and educates the public on staying safe in cyberspace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As Minister Ng Eng Hen spoke about earlier, we have strengthened our defence sector networks through setting up the Defence Cyber Organisation and ensuring that we have a strong core and pipeline of people with the right skills and expertise to do this work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For the rest of our personnel, MINDEF and SAF will inoculate them against hostile information campaigns and fake news, as well as strengthen cybersecurity awareness through enhancing our existing curriculum and learning journeys.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We hope that, collectively, these efforts will help our Servicemen better understand the role of fake news in modern warfare, the steps that they can take in response, and strengthen cyber hygiene as a whole.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For students, issues related to Digital Defence are already in the Ministry of Education's curriculum and will be reinforced through digital literacy and Cyber Wellness programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Students who have played the refreshed game felt it helped them better understand these threats and how they can play a part.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For example, the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) College East student Deshaun Lau shared with us, and I quote, “Playing the game helped me realise that when we face digital threats, we must stay together as a community, and remind one another to take steps to prevent these attacks”, unquote.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Businesses, too, are putting Digital Defence in action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: A workplace design company, Space Matrix, has not only invested in cybersecurity systems, but also trained their staff to keep these threats at bay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They did not fall victim, thanks to the vigilance of their staff, who recognised the false email identification.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The company subsequently finetuned their systems to better protect themselves for the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: While we step up efforts in Digital Defence, the multifaceted threats of today mean that to keep Singapore strong, we need a collective effort where everyone plays a part and takes action across all six pillars of Total Defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Mr Chairman, may I say a few words in Malay, please?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Chairman, the recent maritime and airspace disputes between Singapore and Malaysia have reinforced the importance of Total Defence for us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our security agencies stand ready and vigilant to safeguard our sovereignty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Singaporeans also need to remain united and stand firm on our principles to protect our national interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Therefore, it has been heartening to see how many Singaporeans have taken to social media to counter false claims and show support for Singapore’s position.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: One example is a post by Mr John Lam, who encouraged fellow Singaporeans to remain calm and civil when the maritime dispute between Singapore and Malaysia became tense.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: He used examples from Singapore’s past to show how we, as one people, have overcome our constraints, and came out stronger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For instance, when we were faced with the threats to cut our water supplies, we invested in water filtration and desalination technologies and developed our own NEWater treatment plants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: When faced with a sand import ban, we developed innovative and environmentally-friendly ways of using less sand for reclamation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: What Mr Lam and many others have done embody what Psychological Defence is about – our people staying united and resolving to stand up for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Members of this House, like Ms Cheng Li Hui, have acknowledged the importance of this as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The recent bilateral tensions between Singapore and Malaysia have helped Singaporeans better understand what we stand for, and why it is so important for us to take these positions on upholding our territorial sovereignty and operating within a rules-based international order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our small size and the volatility in our region show how crucial it is for Singaporeans to remain committed to our own defence, and having a strong Singapore Armed Forces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: (In English): I spoke earlier about how the terrorism threat is here to stay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Security agencies will do all we can to prevent an attack, but, even if one takes place, it is important that every Singaporean knows what to do so that we can hold together, and bounce back quickly as a society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We commend ground-up initiatives that put Total Defence in action in this way, such as the example of the young Singaporeans who came together to develop the Bukit Panjang Emergency Preparedness Guide, with the support of Bukit Panjang Community Emergency and Engagement Committee, as Dr Teo Ho Pin had shared.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This complements MHA's SGSecure effort, which continues to build vigilance, cohesion and resilience in the community to deal with a terror attack.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: MINDEF's Total Defence partnerships with organisations, such as the Singapore Red Cross and Temasek Foundation Cares, also equip people with the knowledge and skills that they can apply in a crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: MINDEF has also been actively reaching out to our youths and the wider community on Total Defence, and it is heartening to see how they have rallied around Total Defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The game highlights how simple everyday actions can contribute towards building a strong and cohesive nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The game's developers hope that by doing so, they can inspire their fellow youths to play their part and put Total Defence into action.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, my question is to the Minister of Defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am interested to know how much and to what extent these modifications will be developed in Singapore through our local defence industries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Chairman, there is no change in that sense in our procurement policies where we get the best of class for our needs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But also, when I say for our needs, obviously, a key restriction is manpower.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And if we look at, for example, our ships, the reason why we went to local production, first of all in our frigates, which we did with French DCN, and then we built our own.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even with that, we designed it from conception to operation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because few other nations are able to have the SAF that we have that is able to defend a small island and have to do so with fewer people.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, for the ships, we went in that way.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: From a maintenance point of view, we dealt with the issue by contracting it to some of our strategic partners, private companies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we do not leave it, for example, to the marketplace.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And that is why, over the years, a number of companies have been able to work with MINDEF and SAF to meet our defence needs.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Vikram Nair, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: NS safety remains a priority and we are investing to deal with cyber threats and terrorism.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: These are all important considerations and I thank the Ministry for being on top of it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, I beg leave to withdraw the amendment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head J of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 2017, we celebrated 50 years of National Service (NS) and Singaporeans of all generations joined in.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) has been an integral part of Singapore and we are all either serving National Servicemen (NSmen) or family members of one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, the SAF was set up over 50 years ago and much of the training involved training in jungle warfare which reflected the terrain of our region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, the nature of our region and the nature of our threats have evolved significantly over the years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we start with the threats, the SAF was set up against the backdrop of the Cold War, and the struggle with the communist insurgents in the region was one of the main focuses.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In its place, we see new rivalries and tensions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The strategic competition between the United States (US) and China has intensified and it appears to be a new great power rivalry.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Tensions in the South China Sea continue and no swift resolutions appear to be in sight.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Korean peninsula, probably one of the last legacies of the Cold War, remains volatile.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And although Trump and Kim are having a second summit, there does not appear to be any firm commitment to denuclearise on the part of North Korea.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: India and Pakistan have always had tensions between them, but the events in the last few days are particularly worrying, especially because of how fast the conflict seems to be escalating.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) countries have also been spending more on defence, and these are our immediate neighbours.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fresh in Singaporeans' minds would be the fact that Malaysia still has two vessels in our waters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although both sides have made efforts to de-escalate since, there does not appear to be an easy resolution or end to this matter.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And if matters escalate – we hope it will not be necessary – but the SAF may have to get involved.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other end of the technological spectrum, the threat of terrorism remains present.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are an increasing number of foreign fighters returning to the region from the wars in the Middle East and they remain a potential source of terror here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) has also set up in Indonesia and there were reports of attacks being planned on Singapore from there.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The issue with terror attacks is that they are targeted at the civilian population, unlike conventional warfare, and could strike anyone, anywhere.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against the backdrop of these threats, the SAF faces two primary challenges.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore already has a very significant disadvantage in terms of size in any conflict.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And our only hope appears to be that if we rely more on automation and sophisticated equipment systems, we may be able to compensate for this somewhat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And it is in this context that I ask about the future of the SAF.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In view of the variety of threats we now face, how does SAF ensure it remains an effective fighting force capable of defending Singapore?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What new capabilities will SAF be introducing over the next few years to meet the new security challenges?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I earlier discussed the wide variety of threats SAF was facing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: SAF also has a wide range of resources and capabilities it has developed over the years, as well as a variety of different operations that it engages in.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is necessary to deal with the wider spectrum of threats we are facing, as well as the more messy nature of warfare.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, even if these demands on SAF continue to grow, as mentioned earlier, it faces constraints in terms of having less space to train.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: More and more SAF training areas and camps are being converted to other uses, particularly residential and commercial uses.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The announcement in relation to Paya Lebar Airbase was one example of this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am aware that SAF has adapted to this in many ways.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes the more productive use of land for training, such as multi-storey rifle ranges and centralised conducting of training activities, such as Basic Military Training and reservist training.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: SAF has also leveraged on its good relationships to train in territories overseas and this has helped train in capabilities that we may not be able to train in Singapore as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most NSmen and reservists would have some experience of training overseas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, I remain concerned as more and more training areas are given up for other uses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As mentioned in this year's Budget speech, today's more uncertain world spells greater possibility for tension and even conflict.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Unexpected incidents under such circumstances can result in potentially dangerous unintended and uncontrolled escalation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has rightly continued to stress the need for Singapore to support a stable, rules‐based order founded on international law and norms.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When meeting and engaging with foreign counterparts during peacetime, such as in the Shangri‐La Dialogue, how does MINDEF seek to contribute to the prevention of unintended and uncontrolled escalation of tensions in the region?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: More specifically, what kind of practical cooperation with other militaries regionally has MINDEF engaged in to enhance cooperation and dispel mistrust?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does MINDEF maintain or initiate high‐level military hotlines with the military from other countries to ensure that any potential issues on the ground can be discussed quickly?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, ASEAN is the cornerstone of our regional security architecture.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: It has promoted an avenue for Southeast Asian countries to meet and discuss areas for mutual cooperation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: While most people are familiar with ASEAN as an economic forum, ASEAN is also an important platform to come together on defence matters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The ASEAN Defence Minister's Meeting (ADMM) was one of the primary pillars of these.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In recent years, however, relationships among ASEAN appear to have become more strained for several reasons.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: First, the rivalry between the US and China also seems to be putting pressure on ASEAN countries as some come under pressure to choose in this rivalry.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Second, on matters related to the South China Sea, there appears to be a growing risk of a divide among ASEAN members as some of them are direct claimant states in this matter, while others have differing views and different economic incentives in this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Third, terrorism is a growing security threat and, with fighters returning from the Middle East to the region, there is a pressing need for cooperation to manage this threat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Many countries in the Asia Pacific have overlapping maritime and territorial claims.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As tensions escalate among claimant states, there is a real risk of miscalculation on the ground.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As militaries become more advanced, the cost of any conflict will be grave.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: For example, if fighter planes of one country are perceived to have improperly crossed into the territorial air space of another country and that country responds by shooting down the plane, that could quickly lead to retaliation and escalation and both countries may find themselves on the path to war.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The current exchanges between India and Pakistan are an example of how quickly a conflict can escalate once one party engages in the use of force.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Given the high risk of conflict breaking out, it is important for regional militaries to establish mechanisms to build trust, strengthen confidence and minimise conflict in the region.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This year, fully a third of our Budget goes to Diplomacy and Defence.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is the lion's share of the Budget and, for MINDEF at least, spent in anticipation of actions we hope never to take, and events we hope never to transpire.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, the fact that we are prepared, willing and able will continue to make a difference in the way the odds fall for or against us.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Deterrence is, as the Finance Minister has said, one of the two important prongs of our foreign relations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this, I would like to first ask: what is the role of the SAF in the ongoing bilateral dispute with Malaysia in our Territorial Waters around Tuas?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the meantime, Minister for Defence, Dr Ng Eng Hen, has also told this House how our security personnel will respond to intrusions into Singapore Territorial Waters.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Police Coast Guard, Republic of Singapore Navy and Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore are all part of the protective cover that we have, in defending our waters.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For sure, there is a difference between what we can do, given our military equipment, and what we should do.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Intrusions into our waters have taken place since late November last year.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have seen how these intrusions can lead to accidents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is not something that we had not foreseen.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, we had previously warned our neighbours, the Malaysians, that through these actions of theirs, it poses a threat to safety of navigation in the area.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Overall, our recent dispute with Malaysia has emphasised the need for Singapore to have a credible defence to protect Singapore's sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have made clear our stand, and we have sent strong signals that threats to our sovereignty will not be cost-free.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Patience is a virtue, but patience also has its limits, and it also cannot prevent accidents from taking place, nor does it automatically lead to de-escalation of tensions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And specifically, what are MINDEF and the SAF doing to enhance our defences around Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, NS is a key institution in this country we call home.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Hundreds and thousands of men have served in uniform since 1967 and stand ready to defend the country as operationally-ready NSmen.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This outcome will have a significant impact on manpower-intensive vocations and services, such as the Army, in particular.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some years ago, the Minister shared that part of the solution would be the steady evolution to motorised platforms and equipment that require a lower complement of men and women to man.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And to this end, does the Minister foresee an even greater reliance on unmanned platforms and does the SAF intend to procure such platforms in a weaponised form in larger numbers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, in light of the regional and global environment, it would appear the SAF will continue to play a significant role in various national duties alongside Home Team units.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More recently, the Minister has spoken about ramping up cyber warfare and cyber defence capabilities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are likely to stretch the SAF's manpower requirements even further.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How will the SAF manage the manpower imperatives of these new functions, in addition to its core war-fighting responsibilities, in light of dwindling numbers over the next few years?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: More importantly, the F-35's stealth capabilities can help us maintain air dominance and overcome sophisticated air defence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, the F-35s can fuse sensors and information from different sources, thereby networking our 4th Generation aircrafts and SAF assets together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In short, the acquisition of F-35s can level up the Republic of Singapore Air Force's (RSAF's) capabilities significantly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And despite earlier concerns of the F-35 programme, it has achieved initial operation capability in several countries, including the US.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, given the unprecedented complexity of F-35 as a programme, we can expect it to evolve and mature over time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, the cost of the F-35s can differ, and perhaps decrease, as the F-35 programme becomes more mature.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, it is important for us to purchase the appropriate number of F-35s, with the appropriate capabilities, at the appropriate time.
